rows.send: Cell: heart muscle cell. Basic unit of structure and function. The cell is the smallest unit that can carry out all the activities of life. This heart muscle cell is long and striped. The stripes are protein fibers that shorten to make the cell contract. Like all animal cells it has a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus, but no cell wall.
Stage. Holds the slide. The flat platform where you put the slide. The hole in the middle lets light pass up through the specimen. The specimen must be thin so light can shine through it.

Tissue: heart muscle. Similar cells with one job. A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to do the same job. Animals have 4 main tissue types: muscle, nervous, epithelial and connective tissue. Heart muscle cells are branched and linked end to end, so they contract together as one team.  〔spoken: Tissue: heart muscle. Similar cells with one job. A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to do the same job. Animals have four main tissue types: muscle, nervous, epithelial and connective tissue. Heart muscle cells are branched and linked end to end, so they contract together as one team.〕

Organ: the heart. Several tissues working together. An organ is a structure made of two or more kinds of tissue that work together for a specific job. The heart contains muscle tissue (to pump), nervous tissue (to control the beat), connective tissue and epithelial tissue (lining). Your heart beats about 100,000 times every day.  〔spoken: Organ: the heart. Several tissues working together. An organ is a structure made of two or more kinds of tissue that work together for a specific job. The heart contains muscle tissue, to pump, nervous tissue, to control the beat, connective tissue and epithelial tissue, lining. Your heart beats about one hundred thousand times every day.〕

Coarse adjustment knob. Big focus moves. The large knob moves the stage up or down a lot. Use it only with the LOW-power objective to find the image. On high power it could crash the long objective into the slide.
Common mix-up: A tissue has one main kind of cell. An organ has several kinds of tissue.

Organ system. Organs working together. An organ system is a group of organs that work together to do one big job. The circulatory system equals heart + blood vessels + blood. It carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell. Systems also team up: the respiratory system brings in oxygen, and the circulatory system delivers it.  〔spoken: Organ system. Organs working together. An organ system is a group of organs that work together to do one big job. The circulatory system equals heart, blood vessels and blood. It carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell. Systems also team up: the respiratory system brings in oxygen, and the circulatory system delivers it.〕

Diaphragm. Controls how much light. Opening the diaphragm lets in more light; closing it makes the view dimmer but often clearer for see-through cells. At high power the view gets darker, so you may need to open the diaphragm.
Theodor Schwann. A zoologist who showed that ALL animals are made of cells too. With Schleiden he proposed that cells are the basic unit of all living things.
Rudolf Virchow. A doctor who stated “Omnis cellula e cellula”: every cell comes from another cell. (He built on observations of cell division by Robert Remak.)
Arm. Holds the top and is used to carry it. Carry a microscope with two hands: one hand on the arm, the other under the base. The arm connects the body tube to the base.

Eyepiece (ocular lens). The lens you look through. The eyepiece usually magnifies 10 times . Total magnification equals eyepiece power times objective power. 10 times times 40 times equals 400 times .  〔spoken: Eyepiece, ocular lens. The lens you look through. The eyepiece usually magnifies ten times. Total magnification equals eyepiece power times objective power. Ten times, times forty times, equals four hundred times.〕
Common mix-up: Bigger organisms do not have bigger cells. They have MORE cells.
Common mix-up: Plants have organs too (root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed), but plants are usually NOT described as having “organ systems” like animals do.

Organelle: mitochondrion. Releases energy for the cell. Organelles are tiny structures inside a cell, each with its own job, like the nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes. Mitochondria release energy from food by cellular respiration. The folded inner membrane gives more space for this work. Heart muscle cells are packed with mitochondria because the heart never stops working.

Fine adjustment knob. Small focus moves. The small knob moves the stage just a tiny bit to make the image sharp. At high power (40 times ), use ONLY the fine knob.  〔spoken: Fine adjustment knob. Small focus moves. The small knob moves the stage just a tiny bit to make the image sharp. At high power, forty times, use ONLY the fine knob.〕
Base. Supports the microscope. The heavy bottom keeps the microscope steady. Support the base with one hand whenever you carry the microscope.
Common mix-up: An elephant is bigger than a mouse NOT because its cells are bigger, but because it has far MORE cells! Most animal cells are about the same size.
Stage clips. Hold the slide still. Two metal clips press the slide flat so it does not slide around.

Antonie van Leeuwenhoek. Ground amazing single lenses (up to about 270 times ) and became the first person to see LIVING cells: tiny swimming “animalcules” in pond water, and later bacteria and blood cells.  〔spoken: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek. Ground amazing single lenses, up to about two hundred seventy times, and became the first person to see LIVING cells: tiny swimming “animalcules” in pond water, and later bacteria and blood cells.〕
Common mix-up: “Cell” is the smallest LIVING level. Organelles are parts of a cell; they cannot live on their own.
Common mix-up: Higher magnification does not show MORE of the slide. It shows a smaller area, but bigger.
Revolving nosepiece. Switches objective lenses. Turn it to click a different objective lens into place. Always turn the nosepiece itself, not the objective lenses.
Body tube. Connects eyepiece and objectives. Light travels up through the body tube to your eye. It holds the lenses at the right distance apart.

Organism. A whole living thing. An organism is a complete living thing that can carry out all life processes on its own. A human body is made of about 37 trillion cells, more than 200 kinds of them. A unicellular organism (like a bacterium or paramecium) is just ONE cell, so for it the cell level and the organism level are the same.  〔spoken: Organism. A whole living thing. An organism is a complete living thing that can carry out all life processes on its own. A human body is made of about thirty-seven trillion cells, more than two hundred kinds of them. A unicellular organism, like a bacterium or paramecium, is just ONE cell, so for it the cell level and the organism level are the same.〕
Robert Hooke. Looked at a thin slice of cork with his microscope and saw rows of tiny empty boxes. They reminded him of small rooms, so he named them “cells”.

Light source. Shines light up through the slide. A compound microscope needs light to pass THROUGH the specimen. Older microscopes use a mirror (反光镜) to reflect light instead of a lamp.  〔spoken: Light source. Shines light up through the slide. A compound microscope needs light to pass THROUGH the specimen. Older microscopes use a mirror, 反光镜, to reflect light instead of a lamp.〕
Common mix-up: The “cells” Hooke saw were only the empty walls of dead cork cells. The first person to see LIVING cells was Leeuwenhoek.
Matthias Schleiden. A botanist who studied many plant parts and concluded that ALL plants are made of cells.

Objective lenses. Main magnifying lenses. Most school microscopes have 4 times (low), 10 times (medium) and 40 times (high) objectives. Higher-power objectives are LONGER, so they come very close to the slide. Always start with the lowest-power objective: it shows the largest area and is easiest to focus.  〔spoken: Objective lenses. Main magnifying lenses. Most school microscopes have four times, low, ten times, medium, and forty times, high, objectives. Higher-power objectives are LONGER, so they come very close to the slide. Always start with the lowest-power objective: it shows the largest area and is easiest to focus.〕
The green organelle where photosynthesis happens.

Think of a cell as a city: the nucleus is city hall, mitochondria are power plants, ribosomes are factories, the ER is the roads, the Golgi body is the post office, and lysosomes are the clean-up crew.

Elodea and egg labs. Elodea in salt water: water leaves, chloroplasts clump away from the wall (plasmolysis); tap water brings them back. Vinegar dissolves the eggshell (CO2 bubbles). Corn syrup (hypertonic) shrinks the egg; distilled water (hypotonic) swells it. percent change equals (final minus initial) divided by initial times 100. IV equals type of solution; DV equals mass.  〔spoken: Elodea and egg labs. Elodea in salt water: water leaves, chloroplasts clump away from the wall, plasmolysis; tap water brings them back. Vinegar dissolves the eggshell, C O two bubbles. Corn syrup, hypertonic, shrinks the egg; distilled water, hypotonic, swells it. percent change equals, final minus initial, divided by initial, times one hundred. IV equals type of solution; DV equals mass.〕
Why are viruses usually NOT considered living? They are too small to see. They are not made of cells and can’t reproduce on their own. They can make people sick. They contain genetic material

A cell wraps its membrane around a big particle and brings it in.
Plant and animal cells share a membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm and mitochondria. Only plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and one big central vacuole.
Passive movement through a protein channel, like glucose entering a cell.
A vesicle fuses with the membrane to release insulin outside the cell.
Plant cells have one large one of these for storing water.

In 1665 Robert Hooke saw tiny boxes in cork and called them cells. A few years later Antonie van Leeuwenhoek saw the first living cells swimming in pond water.  〔spoken: In sixteen sixty-five Robert Hooke saw tiny boxes in cork and called them cells. A few years later Antonie van Leeuwenhoek saw the first living cells swimming in pond water.〕
The “powerhouse” that releases energy from food.
mitochondria.
Is it alive? Living things are made of cells, use energy, grow, reproduce, respond to their surroundings and keep their insides stable: homeostasis.
A rigid layer outside the membrane, found in plant cells but not animal cells.

Cell theory and its timeline. 1) All living things are made of one or more cells. 2) The cell is the basic unit of structure and function. 3) All cells come from pre-existing cells. Hooke 1665 (cork, named “cells”), Leeuwenhoek 1670s (first living cells), Schleiden 1838 (plants), Schwann 1839 (animals), Virchow 1855 (cells from cells). Better microscopes made each discovery possible.  〔spoken: Cell theory and its timeline. One. All living things are made of one or more cells. Two. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function. Three. All cells come from pre-existing cells. Hooke sixteen sixty-five, cork, named “cells”; Leeuwenhoek sixteen seventies, first living cells; Schleiden eighteen thirty-eight, plants; Schwann eighteen thirty-nine, animals; Virchow eighteen fifty-five, cells from cells. Better microscopes made each discovery possible.〕
You’ve reviewed cells, cell theory, organelles and transport. Rate yourself on the study map, then take the practice test to see what to study next.

Active transport. Needs energy (ATP): moves things from LOW to HIGH concentration (against the gradient). Protein pumps, like the sodium-potassium pump. Endocytosis equals the membrane wraps around big particles to bring them IN; exocytosis equals vesicles fuse with the membrane to send things OUT.
The sodium-potassium ____ uses ATP to move ions against their gradients.  〔spoken: The sodium-potassium blank uses ATP to move ions against their gradients.〕
chromosomes / DNA.  〔spoken: chromosomes or DNA.〕
cell membrane.
The state when the concentration is the same everywhere.

Organelles and their functions. Nucleus equals control center (DNA). Mitochondria equals release energy from food. Ribosomes equals make proteins. ER equals transport. Golgi equals package and ship proteins. Lysosomes equals break down wastes. Vacuole equals storage. Cell membrane equals controls what enters and leaves. Cell wall equals support. Chloroplast equals photosynthesis.
Passive transport needs no energy. Particles diffuse from high to low concentration, water moves by osmosis, and some molecules slip through protein channels.

Microscopes. Total magnification equals eyepiece times objective (10 times times 40 times equals 400 times ). Start on low power; use the coarse knob only at low power and the fine knob at high power. Wet mount: specimen + drop of water + coverslip lowered at an angle (no air bubbles).  〔spoken: Microscopes. Total magnification equals eyepiece times objective, ten times, times forty times, equals four hundred times. Start on low power; use the coarse knob only at low power and the fine knob at high power. Wet mount: specimen, drop of water and coverslip lowered at an angle, no air bubbles.〕
Particles spreading from high concentration to low concentration.
He looked at cork in 1665 and named the little boxes “cells”.  〔spoken: He looked at cork in sixteen sixty-five and named the little boxes “cells”.〕

Challenge: At 400 times the field of view is about 400 µm wide. A cell stretches across one quarter of it. About how long is the cell? 100 µm. 400 µm. 1,600 µm. 25 µm  〔spoken: Challenge: At four hundred times, the field of view is about four hundred micrometers wide. A cell stretches across one quarter of it. About how long is the cell? One hundred micrometers. Four hundred micrometers. One thousand six hundred micrometers. Twenty-five micrometers〕
independent variable.
The basic unit of structure and function in all living things.

Challenge: Why does diffusion happen faster in warm water than in cold water? Cold water uses ATP. The particles move faster when they have more heat energy. Warm water has no particles. The membrane disappears
chloroplast.
Sort the examples.
ribosomes. Tiny organelles that make proteins. Some float free; some sit on the rough ER. Factories. Ribs equals meat equals protein!
Water follows solute. In a hypertonic solution cells lose water: Elodea plasmolyses and the egg in syrup shrinks. In a hypotonic solution they gain water. Isotonic means no change.
Tiny organelles that build proteins.
Keeping a stable internal environment, like a steady body temperature.
The diffusion of water across a membrane.

Cell analogies (Cell City). Nucleus equals city hall, mitochondria equals power plant, ribosomes equals factories, ER equals roads. Golgi equals post office, lysosomes equals recycling / clean-up crew, vacuole equals water tower / warehouse. Membrane equals border checkpoint, cell wall equals city wall, chloroplasts equals solar power plant.  〔spoken: Cell analogies, Cell City. Nucleus equals city hall, mitochondria equals power plant, ribosomes equals factories, ER equals roads. Golgi equals post office, lysosomes equals recycling or clean-up crew, vacuole equals water tower or warehouse. Membrane equals border checkpoint, cell wall equals city wall, chloroplasts equals solar power plant.〕

Plant vs. animal cells. Both: cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, ER, Golgi body, vacuoles. Plant only: cell wall, chloroplasts, one large central vacuole (boxy shape). Animal: no wall, small vacuoles, lysosomes common, rounder shape.
Challenge: A poison stops a cell from making ATP. Which process stops working? Facilitated diffusion. Diffusion of oxygen. Osmosis. Protein pumps (active transport)
lysosomes.
Sacs of enzymes that break down wastes and worn-out parts.
Virchow’s idea: every cell comes from this.

To see cells we use a microscope. Multiply the eyepiece by the objective: 10 times 40 is 400 times. Use only the fine focus knob at high power.  〔spoken: To see cells we use a microscope. Multiply the eyepiece by the objective: ten times forty is four hundred times. Use only the fine focus knob at high power.〕

Elodea in salt water: the membrane pulls away from the cell wall.
Golgi body (Golgi apparatus).
cytoplasm.

Schleiden said all plants are made of cells, Schwann said all animals are, and Virchow said every cell comes from another cell. Together: the cell theory.
The gas in the bubbles when an egg sits in vinegar.
What happens to a naked egg in corn syrup?
Active transport uses energy, ATP, to pump things from low to high concentration, or to swallow big particles by endocytosis and send things out by exocytosis.
Animal cells can burst in distilled water but plant cells can’t, because animal cells lack this.
nucleolus.
Active transport moves materials in this direction.
The control center that holds the DNA.
organelle.
nucleus.

Hyper-, hypo- and isotonic. Always compare the solution OUTSIDE with the inside of the cell. Water follows solute. Hypertonic, water out (animal: shrivels; plant: plasmolysis). Hypotonic, water in (animal: swells/bursts; plant: turgid). Isotonic, no net movement (0.9 percent saline for blood cells).  〔spoken: Hyper, hypo, and isotonic. Always compare the solution OUTSIDE with the inside of the cell. Water follows solute. Hypertonic, water out, animal: shrivels; plant: plasmolysis. Hypotonic, water in, animal: swells or bursts; plant: turgid. Isotonic, no net movement, zero point nine percent saline for blood cells.〕

Characteristics of life and “Is it a cell?”. Living things are made of cells, use energy, grow and develop, reproduce, respond to stimuli and keep homeostasis. All living things have DNA and can adapt over generations. Viruses are NOT made of cells, so most scientists say they are not alive.
A red blood cell is placed in distilled water. What happens? Water moves in; it swells and may burst. Nothing happens. Water moves out; it shrivels. Salt moves in and it shrinks
plasmolysis.
The first person to see LIVING single-celled organisms, which he called “animalcules”.

Passive transport. No energy needed: particles move from HIGH to LOW concentration (down the gradient). Diffusion (e.g., oxygen in, CO2 out), osmosis equals diffusion of WATER across a membrane. Facilitated diffusion: still high, low, but through a protein channel (e.g., glucose).  〔spoken: Passive transport. No energy needed: particles move from HIGH to LOW concentration, down the gradient. Diffusion, for example, oxygen in, C O two out. Osmosis equals diffusion of WATER across a membrane. Facilitated diffusion: still high, low, but through a protein channel, for example, glucose.〕
concentration gradient.
ribosomes.
cell wall.
stimulus and response.
In diffusion, particles move… Only when the cell spends ATP. From low concentration to high concentration. From high concentration to low concentration. Only into the cell
Who was the first to see LIVING single-celled organisms (“animalcules”)? Robert Hooke. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek. Matthias Schleiden. Rudolf Virchow
The energy molecule cells spend.
An egg goes from 60 g to 75 g. Its percent change in mass.  〔spoken: An egg goes from sixty grams to seventy-five grams. Its percent change in mass.〕
